strengths: Addresses a genuine and underserved problem: orthographic anomalies (hooked-letter substitution, spacing errors) in Hausa, with clear motivation and good coverage of Hausa NLP background.
The 450K+ noisy-clean parallel corpus is a tangible resource contribution, explicitly released under CC-BY-4.0, with source data statistics reported per collection.

Noise generation is not arbitrary: the authors calibrate the synthetic noise distribution (normalized Levenshtein distances) against ~10K real Hausa tweets, and report the noise-function probabilities (Table 2), which strengthens the realism of the synthetic data.

Broad, sensible model comparison (M2M100 variants, AfriTEVA variants, mBART, AfriMBART, mT5, Opus-MT, LSTM baseline) with multiple complementary metrics (BLEU, METEOR, F1, WER, CER), SacreBLEU signature reported, and full training hyperparameters in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

Includes a human evaluation by a native Hausa speaker and honest, concrete error analysis in Appendix D (named-entity substitutions, subject errors, catastrophic failure case), plus a candid limitations section acknowledging synthetic-noise and lack-of-extrinsic-evaluation concerns.
Transferable methodology for other low-resource languages facing similar orthographic variation, which is relevant to the ACL community.
weaknesses: The entire test set is also synthetically corrupted, so all headline metrics (including the best model's 0.86 BLEU / 0.017 CER) measure correction of synthetic noise, not real writing errors. The real tweet data is used only for calibration, never for evaluation, leaving the paper's central claim ('corrects realistic writing anomalies') only indirectly supported.

The human evaluation is thin and internally inconsistent: a single native-speaker annotator on 500 samples, no inter-annotator agreement, and confusing arithmetic (71.6% 'correct' but 57 of those contain hooked-character swaps — which contradicts being 'correct according to the reference'; the 12.5% vs. 27% percentages are ambiguous).

Several anomalous results are reported without analysis or investigation: AfriTEVA-Large collapses (0.12 BLEU) while the smaller variants do far better; AfriMBART achieves 0.82 BLEU yet WER/CER above 1.0; the LSTM baseline has high F1 but very low BLEU. These unexplained anomalies undermine confidence in the experimental analysis.
No significance testing, no report of variance across runs or seeds, and unclear which models used LoRA vs. full fine-tuning, making some comparisons hard to interpret.

Limited technical novelty: synthetic-noise generation plus seq2seq fine-tuning is a well-established recipe in GEC/spell-correction; the contribution is primarily the Hausa resource rather than methodological insight, and there is no comparison to or positioning against existing low-resource correction approaches (e.g., noised-BERT-style denoising, prior African-language GEC work).

Presentation quality issues: typos in the text ('evaluaion', 'performes', 'translaiton', 'the models makes'), a malformed reference (Tukur et al. with placeholder author marks), noise type 'transpose_characters' appears in Table 2 but is never described in the noise-function list, and an incomplete description of the relation between 'incorrect_characters' and 'substitute_characters' noise functions.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem for a widely spoken low-resource language: orthographic anomalies (hooked-letter substitutions and spacing errors) in Hausa digital text, with clear relevance to downstream Hausa NLP.

Construction of a large (450K+) noisy-clean parallel corpus calibrated against a real tweet sample via normalized Levenshtein distance distributions is a reasonable and transparent approach to synthetic data generation, and the noise configuration (Table 2) and training hyperparameters are reported, supporting reproducibility.

Broad comparison across model families (M2M100, AfriTEVA, AfriMBART, mBART, mT5, Opus-MT, LSTM baseline) with a full metric suite (BLEU, METEOR, F1, WER, CER) and a SacreBLEU signature, plus an honest limitations section and qualitative error analysis with translated examples.
The resource (dataset and fine-tuned models, released under CC-BY-4.0) has standalone value for the Hausa NLP community, and the methodology is transferable to other low-resource languages.
weaknesses: The central claim rests entirely on synthetic evaluation: the test set is generated by the same noise pipeline as the training data, and no evaluation on naturally occurring noisy Hausa text is performed, despite the authors possessing ~10,000 real Hausa tweets used for calibration. This leaves the paper's core claim—that the models improve real-world Hausa text quality—unverified.

Missing crucial baselines. A large fraction of the introduced noise (hooked-letter substitutions) is a deterministic one-to-one character mapping that a trivial rule-based normalizer would fix at near-100% accuracy; without this (or other rule-based/dictionary) baselines, it is impossible to judge whether the neural models add value over simple preprocessing.

The human evaluation is underpowered and internally inconsistent: a single annotator, no inter-annotator agreement, unclear accounting (57 samples reported as 12.5% with no clear denominator), and a 27% incorrect rate that is in tension with the reported BLEU 0.86 / F1 0.93, yet this discrepancy is not analyzed.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting across runs; differences between top models may not be meaningful, and several models fail catastrophically (WER/CER > 1 for AfriMBART and AfriTEVA-Large), suggesting training/optimization problems that are noted but not diagnosed.

The 'analysis and categorization of common writing anomalies' contribution is thin: noise categories are described, but no quantitative analysis of actual error frequencies or distributions in authentic Hausa text is provided beyond the distribution-matching figure.

Writing and rigor issues undermine confidence: typos ('evaluaiton', 'performes'), malformed citations ('"" Tukur'), inconsistent listing of noise types (character substitution described twice; transpose_characters appears in Table 2 but not in the noise description), questionable linguistic claims (e.g., calling Hausa 'agglutinative', the 'karya' (to break) gloss), and an unexplained anomaly in the Hedderich et al. citation (2021 vs. NAACL 2022 proceedings).

Limited engagement with the grammatical error correction literature and no GEC-specific evaluation (e.g., span-based Errant-style analysis), so the work sits somewhat disconnected from the relevant methodological literature.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored problem for a truly low-resource language: orthographic normalization (hooked-character substitution and spacing errors) in Hausa, with clear motivation showing how these errors change meaning.

Construction of a large (450k+ pair) noisy-clean parallel corpus with a commendable calibration step: noise parameters were tuned so the normalized Levenshtein distance distribution matches that of ~10k real Hausa tweets, lending credibility to the realism of the synthetic noise.

Breadth of experimentation: nine systems spanning multilingual (M2M100, mBART-Large-50, mT5), African-language-focused (AfriTEVA variants, AfriMBART), and OPUS-MT models, plus an LSTM baseline, with reasonable training details (Appendix A) and a public dataset release under CC-BY-4.0.

Honest error analysis: the human evaluation (native-speaker assessment of 500 outputs) and the qualitative appendix examples candidly expose failure modes (named-entity respellings, meaning-altering hallucinations), and the Limitations section is appropriately thorough.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: noise parameters are published (Table 2), training hyperparameters are given, and evaluation tooling (SacreBLEU signature) is reported.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular with respect to the noise model: both training and test data are produced by the same synthetic noise pipeline. Since the models are trained on exactly the corruption distribution they are evaluated on, the strong scores (e.g., BLEU 0.86) largely measure the ability to invert known noise functions rather than to correct naturally occurring errors. No evaluation on real noisy Hausa text (e.g., the tweets used only for calibration) is reported, which is the missing decisive experiment.

Several reported metric values are internally inconsistent or unexplained and undermine confidence in the results table: AfriMBART achieves near-top BLEU (0.8175) and F1 (0.8817) while reporting WER 1.5763 and CER 2.7170 — error rates well above 1 imply output length pathology that should invalidate the high token-overlap scores, yet this is not discussed or diagnosed; AfriTEVA-Large collapses (BLEU 0.12) while Base and Small perform well, with only speculative explanation. No significance testing or variance reporting is provided.

The human evaluation is thin: a single annotator, 500 samples, and category accounting that is confusing (71.6% 'correct', 27% 'incorrect' where 'core meaning remained intact', 12.5% of correct predictions still containing hooked-character swaps) — the taxonomy and inter-annotator validity are not established.

The contribution claims both 'detection and correction', but only correction is evaluated; no detection-level (error identification) analysis is provided, and the categorized anomaly analysis promised in the contributions is presented only anecdotally rather than as a systematic study.

The contribution is methodologically straightforward: the approach (synthetic noise + seq2seq fine-tuning) closely mirrors established GEC/denoising practice, and no domain-specific techniques are developed; the main novelty is the language coverage and the resource itself.

Presentation quality issues reduce polish: the related work is largely generic low-resource NLP background; there are notable inconsistencies (noise types described in Section 3.1 do not fully match Table 2, e.g., transpose_characters appears only in the table); and the text contains multiple typos ('evaluaiton', 'performes', 'translaiton', stray punctuation).

Extrinsic value is asserted but not demonstrated: no downstream task (MT, sentiment) experiment shows that corrected text improves real applications, which is the practical claim motivating the work (acknowledged in Limitations).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical gap for Hausa NLP (orthographic normalization of hooked characters and spacing errors), with a substantial publicly released resource: >400k noisy-clean parallel pairs under CC-BY-4.0 plus code, supporting reproducibility

Thoughtful noise-calibration methodology: synthetic noise is induced from analysis of naturally noisy Hausa tweets (NaijaSenti), matched via length-bucketed normalized Levenshtein distributions and quantified with a JS distance of 0.14, going beyond naive random-error augmentation

Comprehensive and well-chosen model comparison spanning multilingual (M2M100, mT5, mBART, BART variants), African-language-specific (AfriTeVA, AfriMBART, cheetah), and African-instruction-tuned LLMs (N-ATLaS 8B), with sensible baselines including a prompted GPT-5.1 system

Careful contamination analysis: MinHashLSH overlap filtering with AfriBERTa corpus data and an additional private OOD test set (MultiplEYE translations) that preserves the model hierarchy, addressing the key threat to validity for this kind of resource

Broad downstream evaluation (genre detection, Hausa-English MT with FLORES+ across four translation systems, and instruction following with MasakhaNER/IrokoBench) that goes beyond intrinsic correction metrics and honestly reports that cleaning only partially recovers performance
Transparent limitations section and informative qualitative error analysis in the appendix showing concrete failure modes (named-entity contamination, tense changes, incoherent outputs)
weaknesses: Circular evaluation concern: both training and test data use the same synthetic noise generator, so results measure correction of artificially injected noise rather than naturally occurring Hausa errors; there is no evaluation on a held-out set of genuinely noisy real-world Hausa text, leaving the central practical claim only partially validated

Human evaluation is thin: a single annotator, 500 binary-labeled samples, with ambiguity about which model was evaluated (the text says 'focused more on AfriTeVA' while claiming evaluation of 'the best model'), and no inter-annotator agreement or statistical treatment

Several results are anomalous or under-explained: AfriMBART's WER/CER exceed 1.0 without discussion; downstream gains are small and sometimes incidental (e.g., Law 78→82, sentiment showing no difference) with no significance testing, weakening the claim of 'significant impact on downstream tasks'

The error-distribution derivation is loosely specified: how cluster-derived error statistics map to the fixed probabilities in Table 1 is not clearly documented, and the statement that changes 'are irreversible using a rule-based system' is confusing
Dependence on proprietary models (GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.4) reduces reproducibility of those baselines and downstream results, and model naming is inconsistent across the paper

Some claims appear overstated (e.g., 'first set of tools for correcting writing anomalies in Hausa' despite related normalization work such as Lusito et al. 2023 for low-resource languages), and there are presentation issues including rendering of the hooked Hausa characters and a confusing description of train/validation/test split sizes

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underserved need: orthographic normalization for Hausa is a real bottleneck for low-resource NLP, and the paper fills a clear resource gap with a large (400k+ pair) noisy-clean parallel corpus released under CC-BY-4.0 alongside code, supporting reproducibility.

The synthetic noise generation is more careful than typical: error types are derived from analysis of naturally noisy Hausa tweets (NaijaSenti) via lexicon/OOV detection and Levenshtein-based clustering, and the synthetic noise distribution is calibrated against the real noise distribution using a JS distance (0.14), with the procedure and noise probabilities documented in Table 1.

Model comparison is reasonably broad (M2M100, AfriTeVA variants, AfriMBART, mT5, cheetah, N-ATLaS, plus copy/LSTM/GPT baselines) and includes practical considerations such as contamination analysis via MinHashLSH overlaps and an out-of-domain evaluation on private, unpublished MultiplEYE translations, which shows the model hierarchy is preserved.

The downstream impact analysis (genre detection, Hausa-English MT with four systems, and LLM instruction following including MasakhaNER and IrokoBench tasks) is a useful contribution beyond the correction task itself, and the paper is honest that cleaning does not fully recover original performance (e.g., NER 0.64 -> 0.19 -> 0.37; MGSM not recovered).

A native-speaker human evaluation of 500 samples is included, and the Limitations section candidly identifies the main weaknesses (synthetic noise projected onto clean texts, genre mismatch, automatic-metric-only downstream evaluation).
weaknesses: The central claim - that the models correct realistic Hausa writing anomalies - is not directly validated. All intrinsic evaluation is against synthetically generated noise, so the models may largely be learning to invert the specific noise generator rather than correct naturally occurring errors. A test on genuinely noisy text (e.g., held-out tweets with native-speaker-validated references) is missing, and this is the paper's most significant methodological gap.

The noise calibration is partially circular: error distributions are derived from a single ~10k tweet seed set, and the synthetic data is then matched to that same distribution, limiting what the JS-distance match actually demonstrates about realism. The native-speaker inspection of generated noise is described as 'non-exhaustive' with no quantification.

Inconsistencies between results and claims undermine confidence: the text states M2M100 obtains 'the best scores across all metrics' while Table 2 shows N-ATLaS best on BLEU, F1, and CER; AfriMBART's WER/CER exceed 1 (1.862/1.825) with no explanation; and the human evaluation section is confusingly written (evaluation 'focused more on AfriTeVA' despite an earlier tie claim, and the 71.6% agreement sits oddly against BLEU ~0.85-0.89 without reconciliation).

No statistical significance testing is reported for model comparisons or downstream gains; some downstream results are small and explicitly acknowledged as incidental (e.g., law 78->82), and the genre-detection deltas (80/78/81 with overlapping std devs) are weak evidence of impact.

Several presentation issues hurt clarity and polish: typographical errors ('Our the findings', 'English translaiton'), undefined hooked characters rendered as blanks in the text, an unclear claim of 'first set of tools' for Hausa correction without adequate positioning against prior text-normalization work (e.g., SchAmane, Ligurian normalization, which are cited only as background), and unspecified GPT model versions/API details for the GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.4 baselines.
Human evaluation is limited to a single native speaker, 500 samples, and binary judgments; inter-annotator agreement and coverage of error types are not reported.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: orthographic normalization for Hausa, a widely spoken but under-resourced language, with clear relevance to low-resource NLP.
Substantial new resource: a 400k+ noisy-clean parallel Hausa dataset, released publicly under CC-BY-4.0 with code, which is likely the most broadly useful artifact of the paper.

Careful dataset calibration methodology: noise distributions are fit against naturally noisy Twitter data (NaijaSenti) using DBSCAN clustering and Jensen-Shannon distance matching, and a native speaker inspects generated noise across genres.

Broad and reasonably rigorous model comparison across multilingual, African-language, and proprietary models, with multiple automatic metrics (BLEU, METEOR, F1, WER, CER) plus a human evaluation of 500 samples by a native speaker.
Concrete attempts to address contamination: MinHashLSH overlap checks against AfriBERTa pretraining data and a held-out private OOD test set from MultiplEYE that preserves the model hierarchy.
Downstream evaluation spans four tasks (genre classification, sentiment, MT, instruction-following/NER), giving a more nuanced picture of when correction helps than most normalization papers provide.
Honest Limitations section acknowledging synthetic-noise domain mismatch and metric-only downstream evaluation, and candid error analysis in Appendix B.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity: both training and (in-domain) test sets use the same synthetic noise generator, so headline results (e.g., BLEU 0.886, WER 0.079) likely overstate performance on naturally noisy text. The OOD set mitigates this but is small (10k words) and human verification of the noise realism is described as 'non-exhaustive'.

Inconsistencies between claims and evidence: the abstract and Section 5 claim correction 'significantly' improves downstream tasks, but several results are flat or mixed (sentiment 78% vs 78%; AfriMGSM 49 vs 49; facts 68 vs 68; NLI 64 vs 66), and the Results section contradicts Table 2 by stating M2M100 obtains 'the best scores across all metrics' when N-ATLaS is best. The Table 2 caption says GPT-5.1 is 'comparable to the baseline of doing no transformation' despite scoring 0.595 BLEU vs 0.293 for the copy baseline.

Human evaluation is thin: a single annotator, 500 samples, binary judgments, and the stated protocol is confusingly described (stating a 'strong tie' between M2M and N-ATLaS, then focusing the evaluation on AfriTeVA). Inter-annotator agreement and clearer adjudication criteria are needed.

Data integrity concerns: 'The validation and training sets each contain 5,000 sentences' appears to be an error (where is the test split?); anomalous WER/CER values above 1.8 for AfriMBART suggest degenerate generations without discussion; the paper states the noise process 'repeated until... match[es]' Twitter distances but the search procedure is underspecified.

Reproducibility gaps despite code release: the proprietary baselines (GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, Google Translate) are non-reproducible, contamination in these models is acknowledged but unquantified, and no significance testing is reported for downstream comparisons (some differences are within reported standard deviations).

Novelty of method is modest: fine-tuning off-the-shelf seq2seq models on synthetic noise is a well-established recipe (cf. Ligurian normalization, SchAmane, etc.); the contribution rests mainly on the dataset and the Hausa-specific analysis, which limits main-conference impact.
Writing quality issues throughout ('Our the findings indicate', 'translaiton', inconsistent hedging) and an incomplete Limitations list (items end at 3) suggest the paper needed another editing pass.
